title: Brush Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Brush wells have a median depth of 80 ft, with typical completed-well costs of $8,800-$16,400.
h1: What Brush, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Brush means dealing with a shallow, productive well area, but the local records still have important gaps. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 1,713 permitted wells, with 1,233 listed as constructed. A total of 1,266 report depth, while only 241 report pump yield and 59 report static water level.

The typical local well is much shallower than the deepest record suggests. The median depth is 80 feet, and the middle half runs from 57 to 103 feet. That is useful for budgeting, but the permit record—not a guarantee—should guide the investigation of a specific lot.

sections.heading: Brush wells are usually shallow, but the ground still matters
sections.html:
Brush-area wells have a median reported depth of 80 feet. Half of the wells with depth data fall between 57 and 103 feet, and 67% are under 100 feet. Another 29% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The local 90th-percentile depth is 130 feet, while the deepest record reaches 1,625 feet.

That spread matters when you request a drilling bid. Alluvium and plains sedimentary rock commonly make the median-depth scenario less complicated than fractured granite, but a driller still has to account for the parcel, casing, grout, access, and the formation actually encountered. Nearby records in Snyder, Hillrose, Fort Morgan, Blue Sky, Saddle Ridge, and Log Lane Village can provide context, not a promise for your lot.

sections.heading: Most Brush wells report strong yield, with a data warning
sections.html:
Among the 241 local records that report pump yield, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 1,100.0 gallons per minute. Records show 88% producing more than 15 gallons per minute, 11% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 1% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

This is a favorable yield pattern for a buyer, but it is not a guarantee because most permitted wells do not report a pump yield. Ask for the well construction record, pump test information, and any production history. A household well also has a 35 gpm exempt-well pumping limit, so a high-yield formation does not automatically mean unrestricted use.

sections.heading: Brush water levels appear shallow in the available records
sections.html:
The median static water level is 19 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 14 to 25 feet. That means a buyer may encounter groundwater relatively close to grade, but the static measurement is not the same as the water available during pumping. Well depth, casing, pump setting, seasonal conditions, and nearby withdrawals still matter.

The reported decade series does not suggest a dropping water table in this dataset. Median depth to water was 23 feet in the 1960s, 18 feet in the 2010s, and 15 feet in the 2020s. Only 59 wells report static water level, so treat that pattern as local evidence rather than a site-specific forecast. Have the existing well measured and tested under normal use.

sections.heading: A long permit history, with Canfield prominent in the records
sections.html:
Brush has a long recorded well history. Permits were issued in the 1950s, 1960s, 1970s, 1980s, 1990s, 2000s, 2010s, and 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. The records include domestic or household wells at 36%, stock wells at 15%, irrigation wells at 20%, and monitoring wells at 18%.

Canfield Drilling Company, also listed as Canfield, Harold E, appears on 197 records. Authorized, listed as Pe, Pg, appears on 149, and Canfield, Leslie George appears on 139. Those names show who appears often in the permit history; they do not establish current availability, pricing, or workmanship. Confirm the permit status and intended use through Colorado DWR before closing or building.

sections.heading: A Brush well budget starts around the shallow local median
sections.html:
For Brush ground described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the local median depth of 80 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $2,800-$4,400. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $8,800-$16,400.

Use that range as a planning number, not a fixed bid. The final price can change with access, casing and grout requirements, pump size, trench length, electrical service, water testing, and the actual depth reached. Get a written scope that separates drilling from completion and identifies what happens if the hole must go deeper or the site cannot produce an acceptable well.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic separation, and the building plan
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records deserve attention before purchase. Within about 10 miles of Brush, the data show 20 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are no historic mine features in the mapped set. These records do not prove contamination at a parcel, so test the existing well and review nearby site history rather than relying on the map alone.

Low yield and dry-hole risk are not visible from the median alone, especially because only 241 records report yield. Confirm the well permit, construction, casing, grout, pump, and maintenance history. Before placing a house or septic system, verify setbacks, soil conditions, access for a rig, and the water-use rules for the proposed use. A household well may also require an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: What to do before buying or building near Brush
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s DWR permit number and compare it with nearby records. Request a current production test, static water-level reading, laboratory water test, and inspection of the pump and pressure system. The local numbers point to a shallow, generally productive setting, but the limited yield reporting means the individual well controls the decision.

For a vacant lot, have a driller review access, likely depth, casing and grout, electrical routing, trenching, and the proposed septic and house locations before you set a budget. Also confirm that the permit allows the intended household, stock, irrigation, or other use. Nearby communities such as Snyder and Fort Morgan can help with regional comparison, but a neighboring well is the better guide to conditions at this specific property.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Brush, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Brush is 80 feet. The middle half runs from 57 to 103 feet, and 67% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Depth still varies by parcel: the deepest record is 1,625 feet, so use nearby permits and a driller’s review rather than assuming the median applies exactly.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Brush, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At Brush’s 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,800-$4,400. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,800-$16,400. Access, casing, grout, electrical distance, pump requirements, and final depth can move the actual bid.

faq.q: Do Brush wells produce enough water for a home?
faq.a: Reported yields are strong: the median is 20.0 gallons per minute, and 88% of records with yield data report more than 15 gallons per minute. However, only 241 wells report pump yield, so the statistic is not a guarantee for an untested property. Review the well permit, test production, and confirm the permitted household use before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Brush, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from well depth or yield. Within about 10 miles, records show 20 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well through a certified laboratory, review the property and nearby environmental history, and repeat testing when ownership or land use changes.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Brush, Colorado?
faq.a: The available static-level records do not show a dropping trend. Median depth to water was 23 feet in the 1960s, 18 feet in the 2010s, and 15 feet in the 2020s. Only 59 wells report static water level, so this series is limited. Measure the property’s well directly and compare it with nearby permits.
